analysis.one_liner: Adds a $1,000 fee to electric vehicle sales to fund highways.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill has received no further action from the committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new federal excise tax: $1,000 on the sale of every electric vehicle and $550 on the sale of a large battery module meant for an electric vehicle. The money collected would be transferred to the Highway Trust Fund, the pot of gas-tax money that pays for roads and bridges. The stated idea is that electric vehicle owners use the roads but pay little or nothing in federal gasoline taxes, so they should contribute to road upkeep at purchase. Hybrid vehicles that also burn gasoline would be exempt, and the tax would apply to sales after the end of 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the Highway Trust Fund and everyone who relies on federally funded roads would gain a new revenue stream, and owners of gasoline-powered vehicles would see electric vehicles become relatively more expensive compared to their cars. Oil and gas producers and traditional gasoline-vehicle makers would gain indirectly, because the tax raises the cost of the competing technology.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a $1,000 excise tax on each electric vehicle sold and a $550 excise tax on battery modules weighing over 1,000 pounds intended for electric vehicles, effective for sales after December 31, 2025.

All money collected under the new taxes must be transferred to the Highway Trust Fund, which finances surface transportation programs, so the revenue is earmarked for roads rather than general spending.

The tax targets a genuine gap in road funding: federal highway money comes chiefly from the gasoline tax, and battery-electric vehicles pay little or none of it, so the bill makes new EV buyers contribute at the point of sale.
Hybrids that combine a gasoline engine with a rechargeable battery are exempt, so the tax falls only on fully battery-powered vehicles.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of new electric vehicles, who would pay $1,000 more per vehicle at purchase (the tax is imposed on the manufacturer or importer but passed on in the vehicle's price), and buyers of large EV battery modules, who would pay $550. Electric vehicle and battery manufacturers would face reduced demand and a new tax liability on each sale.
analysis.who_pays_short: New electric vehicle buyers and EV makers

drawbacks.text: A flat $1,000 fee at purchase charges every EV buyer the same regardless of how many miles they drive, unlike a per-mile charge or a gasoline-tax-equivalent, so a low-mileage EV owner could pay far more than the gas taxes they avoided while a high-mileage one pays less than they should — a poorly matched substitute for the per-gallon tax it replaces.
The tax raises the price of electric vehicles, the cleaner alternative to gasoline cars, and would likely slow EV adoption, working against emissions and air-quality goals.

A one-time purchase fee does not fix the Highway Trust Fund's underlying problem, which is that gas-tax revenue erodes as vehicles become more efficient and as electrification spreads; the fund would still face a shortfall, making this a partial and one-shot patch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The fairness argument behind the bill is real: electric vehicle owners use the roads but pay almost none of the federal gasoline tax that funds them. But the bill's fix is blunt. A flat $1,000 hit at purchase bears no relationship to how much road a buyer actually uses, it falls on the cleaner vehicle technology at the moment federal policy has been encouraging people to buy it, and it does little for the Highway Trust Fund's long-term revenue problem. A per-mile fee or an electricity-based equivalent would match road use far better.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Deb Fischer introduced the Fair SHARE Act of 2025 on February 12, 2025, joined by Senators Pete Ricketts and Cynthia Lummis.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the record since then.
The bill's cosponsor list shows two cosponsors, both Senate Republicans, in a chamber with 55 Republicans and 47 Democrats or independents.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet: electric vehicle buyers pay no new fee and the Highway Trust Fund gets no new revenue. The status quo, under which EV buyers contribute little to road funding but also pay no new tax, is preserved for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EV buyers pay nothing yet; status quo holds

for.name: Sen. Deb Fischer
for.role: U.S. Senator from Nebraska; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on February 12, 2025.

against.role: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since it was referred on February 12, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and both cosponsors are Senate Republicans (2 of 55 Republican senators signed on); no Democrat has joined, and no vote has occurred to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill taxes each EV sale $1,000 and large battery modules $550, raising the price of their products and likely cutting sales. Their loss is shared by the ordinary buyers who pay the tax, so their interests run together here.

By making electric vehicles $1,000 more expensive, the bill keeps gasoline-powered vehicles relatively cheaper, protecting gasoline demand. The industry's relative gain comes out of EV buyers' pockets.
New tax revenue must flow into the Highway Trust Fund, which finances road and bridge work, creating a modest additional stream of funded projects.

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors, no Democratic support, and no committee action more than a year after introduction, the bill looks unlikely to advance. Bills that sit in the Finance Committee without a markup at this stage of a Congress rarely reach the floor; the most realistic path to any action would be if a highway funding or tax package picked up the idea, which has not happened.
